content.text:
The main difference is that **`Media Lab Prototype` is a visual/demo application**, while **`Media-Lab_Manager/Media Lab Front` is the maintained frontend connected to the real backend and database**.

### 1. Architecture

| Area | Media Lab Prototype | Git repository frontend |
|---|---|---|
| Page structure | One generic HTML shell with dynamic rendering through `js/pages.js` | Separate HTML pages under `pages/` and `pages/admin/` |
| Rendering | `#app` is rebuilt dynamically for each page | Static page markup with page-specific JavaScript |
| Styling | Mostly one shared `css/styles.css` | Shared `css/global.css` plus page-specific stylesheets |
| State | One localStorage object: `mlmPrototypeState` | Backend state through `js/api.js`; limited localStorage only for cart/request handoff |
| Runtime | Can run from a static file server | Must run through the Python integration server for real API/auth behavior |

### 2. Authentication and authorization

Prototype:

- Uses a mock login.
- Has a student/admin mode toggle.
- Allows switching roles locally.
- Stores the selected user and role in localStorage.
- Does not verify credentials or permissions.

Git frontend:

- Uses the real Krea email plus four-digit PIN flow.
- Calls `/api/auth/login`.
- Uses an HttpOnly session cookie.
- Calls `/api/auth/me` to restore the session.
- Uses `session.js` to enforce authentication, staff access, and admin access.
- Admin access is determined by the backend role, not by a frontend toggle.
- Supports logout/session expiry through the existing API.

### 3. Data source

Prototype data is hardcoded in `Media Lab Prototype/js/app.js`, including:

- JoyBoy as the default user.
- Six sample equipment records.
- Three sample requests.
- Three sample notifications.
- Sample audit and outbox records.
- Sample settings.

The Git frontend loads data from the backend:

- Equipment from `/api/equipment`.
- Requests from `/api/requests`.
- Dashboard information from `/api/dashboard`.
- Settings from `/api/settings`.
- Audit history from `/api/audit/...`.
- Outbox events from `/api/outbox`.

The Git frontend does not treat the prototype’s sample camera, user, booking, or availability values as authoritative.

### 4. Equipment model

Prototype equipment includes explicit frontend fields such as:

```js
{
  id,
  name,
  category,
  brand,
  asset,
  status,
  detail
}
```

The actual database currently stores fields such as:

- `id`
- `asset_code`
- `name`
- `description`
- `serial_number`
- `status`
- `location`

The database does not currently have dedicated `category`, `brand`, or quantity fields. The Git frontend therefore derives categories such as Cameras, Lenses, Audio, Lighting, and Accessories from equipment names for presentation and filtering.

This means:

- Prototype categories and brands are direct fields.
- Git frontend categories and brands are currently inferred.
- Backend status and IDs remain authoritative in the Git version.

### 5. Catalog behavior

Prototype:

- Uses local mock equipment.
- Filtering happens entirely in memory.
- The admin catalog is read-only.
- Students can add equipment to the local cart.
- Availability is based on hardcoded statuses.

Git frontend:

- Loads equipment from the real API.
- Sends search and availability filters to the backend where supported.
- Performs category/brand filtering in the browser because those fields are not currently in the database.
- Uses real equipment IDs.
- Uses backend availability/status values.
- Stores only the temporary booking cart in localStorage.

### 6. Booking flow

Prototype:

- Uses localStorage state.
- Creates a local request object.
- Does not contact the backend.
- Applies the loan duration setting locally.
- Directly modifies local request status.

Git frontend:

- Converts the booking form into ISO-8601 timestamps.
- Validates date order and the 72-hour limit in the browser.
- Sends requests through `mlmApi.createRequest()`.
- The backend revalidates dates, ownership, availability, and overlaps.
- Equipment reservation state is persisted in SQLite.
- Backend status transitions determine what the user sees afterward.

### 7. Booking form design

Prototype:

- Uses `datetime-local` controls.
- Uses a simple two-column form.
- Uses a prototype settings value for loan duration.

Git frontend:

- Uses separate date and time controls for pickup and return.
- Converts them into backend-compatible ISO timestamps.
- Keeps purpose and notes fields connected to the real request payload.
- Uses the backend’s configured validation rules.

### 8. User history

Prototype:

- Displays local request data.
- Filters All, Current, Pending, and Past requests from local state.
- Uses local request IDs and mock statuses.
- Does not use server-side ownership enforcement.

Git frontend:

- Requests the signed-in user’s requests from `/api/requests`.
- The backend forces student requests to belong to the authenticated session.
- Displays real request items and time windows.
- Uses real workflow statuses such as `pending`, `approved`, `pickup_pending`, `picked_up`, `returned`, `rejected`, and `cancelled`.
- Keeps extension, pickup, return, and cancellation operations tied to backend endpoints.

### 9. Pickup pass

Prototype:

- Builds the pass from local request data.
- Uses sample user and equipment information.
- Updates local state when pickup is confirmed.

Git frontend:

- Loads the booking by ID through the backend.
- Shows the authenticated requester and real request items.
- Displays real pickup and return windows.
- Uses backend request status to determine whether the pass is available.
- Does not currently have a separate backend notification service or QR validation service.

### 10. Return and damage reporting

Prototype:

- Updates the local request object.
- Stores return condition and damage notes in localStorage.
- Does not send damage information to the server.

Git frontend:

- Loads the request and its actual items from the API.
- Sends return data to `/api/requests/:id/return`.
- Supports condition, damage flag, notes, and return time.
- Uses the backend to update equipment status to available or damaged.
- Can use `/api/request-items/:id/damage` for staff damage reports.
- File/photo upload remains limited because the current backend does not provide a file-upload endpoint.

### 11. Extension requests

Prototype:

- Uses local data and prototype state.
- Admin schedule changes update local request windows.
- Student and admin behavior is simulated locally.

Git frontend:

- Uses the real `/api/requests/:id/extensions` endpoint.
- The server validates the request owner, date ordering, and permissions.
- Extension windows are persisted in the database.
- Admin review still depends on the existing server request/window model rather than a separate prototype-only state object.

### 12. Notifications

Prototype:

- Has a dedicated local notification array.
- Supports sample approval, pickup reminder, and system messages.
- Mark-as-read only updates local state.
- Notification counts are based on the local array.

Git frontend:

- Does not currently have a dedicated notification API or notification worker.
- Derives the visible notification experience primarily from request data.
- Uses backend request statuses and timestamps.
- The backend README identifies notification delivery as a future/outside-server feature.

### 13. Admin interface

Prototype:

- Has a single dynamically rendered Admin Console page.
- Includes overview statistics, equipment, requests, audit, and settings sections.
- Uses local mock data.
- Uses local controls for approving, rejecting, and adjusting windows.
- Has a local Reset Demo control.

Git frontend:

- Uses separate protected admin pages:
  - `pages/admin/dashboard.html`
  - `pages/admin/equipment.html`
  - `pages/admin/requests.html`
  - `pages/admin/history.html`
  - `pages/admin/settings.html`
  - `pages/admin/frontend-health.html`
- Uses staff/admin role gates.
- Equipment and requests are loaded from backend endpoints.
- Approval/rejection uses real API mutations.
- Settings use `/api/settings`.
- Dashboard uses `/api/dashboard`.
- Sidebar navigation is shared and normalized through `js/nav.js`.

### 14. Settings

Prototype:

- Stores settings locally.
- Supports loan duration and notification frequency.
- Does not persist settings to the server.

Git frontend:

- Reads from `/api/settings`.
- Updates through `/api/settings` with PATCH.
- Uses the backend’s supported fields:
  - `standardLoanHours`
  - `returnReminderHours`
  - `notifyStaff`
  - `notifyStudents`
- Requires administrator authorization.

### 15. Audit and outbox

Prototype:

- Displays local sample audit and outbox arrays.
- No persistence beyond localStorage.

Git backend:

- Creates audit records for workflow changes.
- Creates outbox events for operations such as request creation, approval, pickup, extension, and return.
- Exposes them through `/api/audit/...` and `/api/outbox`.
- The maintained frontend has a Frontend Health/admin surface documenting these integrations, while full notification delivery remains a backend expansion area.

### 16. Visual differences

The Git frontend has adapted much of the prototype’s visual language, but it is not structurally identical:

- Prototype uses a single generated top navigation shell.
- Git frontend uses separate page headers and admin sidebars.
- Prototype uses sample icons and local visual placeholders.
- Git frontend uses backend-driven labels and real IDs.
- Prototype’s admin layout is a single console view.
- Git frontend separates admin functions into maintainable pages.
- Prototype’s cards and tables are directly generated by `pages.js`.
- Git frontend keeps markup in individual HTML files so existing functionality and debugging remain clearer.

### 17. Important limitation

The prototype represents the intended design and interaction model. The Git frontend represents the real application contract.

Therefore, the following prototype features should not be copied directly into production without backend support:

- Mock student/admin role switching.
- Hardcoded availability.
- Local request approval.
- Local notifications.
- Fake equipment quantities.
- Fake audit/outbox data.
- Static booking IDs.
- Static pickup passes.
- Local-only reset behavior.

The Git version should continue using the Python server and SQLite database as the source of truth.

The main difference is that **`Media Lab Prototype` is a visual/demo application**, while **`Media-Lab_Manager/Media Lab Front` is the maintained frontend connected to the real backend and database**.

### 1. Architecture

| Area | Media Lab Prototype | Git repository frontend |
|---|---|---|
| Page structure | One generic HTML shell with dynamic rendering through `js/pages.js` | Separate HTML pages under `pages/` and `pages/admin/` |
| Rendering | `#app` is rebuilt dynamically for each page | Static page markup with page-specific JavaScript |
| Styling | Mostly one shared `css/styles.css` | Shared `css/global.css` plus page-specific stylesheets |
| State | One localStorage object: `mlmPrototypeState` | Backend state through `js/api.js`; limited localStorage only for cart/request handoff |
| Runtime | Can run from a static file server | Must run through the Python integration server for real API/auth behavior |

### 2. Authentication and authorization

Prototype:

- Uses a mock login.
- Has a student/admin mode toggle.
- Allows switching roles locally.
- Stores the selected user and role in localStorage.
- Does not verify credentials or permissions.

Git frontend:

- Uses the real Krea email plus four-digit PIN flow.
- Calls `/api/auth/login`.
- Uses an HttpOnly session cookie.
- Calls `/api/auth/me` to restore the session.
- Uses `session.js` to enforce authentication, staff access, and admin access.
- Admin access is determined by the backend role, not by a frontend toggle.
- Supports logout/session expiry through the existing API.

### 3. Data source

Prototype data is hardcoded in `Media Lab Prototype/js/app.js`, including:

- JoyBoy as the default user.
- Six sample equipment records.
- Three sample requests.
- Three sample notifications.
- Sample audit and outbox records.
- Sample settings.

The Git frontend loads data from the backend:

- Equipment from `/api/equipment`.
- Requests from `/api/requests`.
- Dashboard information from `/api/dashboard`.
- Settings from `/api/settings`.
- Audit history from `/api/audit/...`.
- Outbox events from `/api/outbox`.

The Git frontend does not treat the prototype’s sample camera, user, booking, or availability values as authoritative.

### 4. Equipment model

Prototype equipment includes explicit frontend fields such as:

```js
{
  id,
  name,
  category,
  brand,
  asset,
  status,
  detail
}
```

The actual database currently stores fields such as:

- `id`
- `asset_code`
- `name`
- `description`
- `serial_number`
- `status`
- `location`

The database does not currently have dedicated `category`, `brand`, or quantity fields. The Git frontend therefore derives categories such as Cameras, Lenses, Audio, Lighting, and Accessories from equipment names for presentation and filtering.

This means:

- Prototype categories and brands are direct fields.
- Git frontend categories and brands are currently inferred.
- Backend status and IDs remain authoritative in the Git version.

### 5. Catalog behavior

Prototype:

- Uses local mock equipment.
- Filtering happens entirely in memory.
- The admin catalog is read-only.
- Students can add equipment to the local cart.
- Availability is based on hardcoded statuses.

Git frontend:

- Loads equipment from the real API.
- Sends search and availability filters to the backend where supported.
- Performs category/brand filtering in the browser because those fields are not currently in the database.
- Uses real equipment IDs.
- Uses backend availability/status values.
- Stores only the temporary booking cart in localStorage.

### 6. Booking flow

Prototype:

- Uses localStorage state.
- Creates a local request object.
- Does not contact the backend.
- Applies the loan duration setting locally.
- Directly modifies local request status.

Git frontend:

- Converts the booking form into ISO-8601 timestamps.
- Validates date order and the 72-hour limit in the browser.
- Sends requests through `mlmApi.createRequest()`.
- The backend revalidates dates, ownership, availability, and overlaps.
- Equipment reservation state is persisted in SQLite.
- Backend status transitions determine what the user sees afterward.

### 7. Booking form design

Prototype:

- Uses `datetime-local` controls.
- Uses a simple two-column form.
- Uses a prototype settings value for loan duration.

Git frontend:

- Uses separate date and time controls for pickup and return.
- Converts them into backend-compatible ISO timestamps.
- Keeps purpose and notes fields connected to the real request payload.
- Uses the backend’s configured validation rules.

### 8. User history

Prototype:

- Displays local request data.
- Filters All, Current, Pending, and Past requests from local state.
- Uses local request IDs and mock statuses.
- Does not use server-side ownership enforcement.

Git frontend:

- Requests the signed-in user’s requests from `/api/requests`.
- The backend forces student requests to belong to the authenticated session.
- Displays real request items and time windows.
- Uses real workflow statuses such as `pending`, `approved`, `pickup_pending`, `picked_up`, `returned`, `rejected`, and `cancelled`.
- Keeps extension, pickup, return, and cancellation operations tied to backend endpoints.

### 9. Pickup pass

Prototype:

- Builds the pass from local request data.
- Uses sample user and equipment information.
- Updates local state when pickup is confirmed.

Git frontend:

- Loads the booking by ID through the backend.
- Shows the authenticated requester and real request items.
- Displays real pickup and return windows.
- Uses backend request status to determine whether the pass is available.
- Does not currently have a separate backend notification service or QR validation service.

### 10. Return and damage reporting

Prototype:

- Updates the local request object.
- Stores return condition and damage notes in localStorage.
- Does not send damage information to the server.

Git frontend:

- Loads the request and its actual items from the API.
- Sends return data to `/api/requests/:id/return`.
- Supports condition, damage flag, notes, and return time.
- Uses the backend to update equipment status to available or damaged.
- Can use `/api/request-items/:id/damage` for staff damage reports.
- File/photo upload remains limited because the current backend does not provide a file-upload endpoint.

### 11. Extension requests

Prototype:

- Uses local data and prototype state.
- Admin schedule changes update local request windows.
- Student and admin behavior is simulated locally.

Git frontend:

- Uses the real `/api/requests/:id/extensions` endpoint.
- The server validates the request owner, date ordering, and permissions.
- Extension windows are persisted in the database.
- Admin review still depends on the existing server request/window model rather than a separate prototype-only state object.

### 12. Notifications

Prototype:

- Has a dedicated local notification array.
- Supports sample approval, pickup reminder, and system messages.
- Mark-as-read only updates local state.
- Notification counts are based on the local array.

Git frontend:

- Does not currently have a dedicated notification API or notification worker.
- Derives the visible notification experience primarily from request data.
- Uses backend request statuses and timestamps.
- The backend README identifies notification delivery as a future/outside-server feature.

### 13. Admin interface

Prototype:

- Has a single dynamically rendered Admin Console page.
- Includes overview statistics, equipment, requests, audit, and settings sections.
- Uses local mock data.
- Uses local controls for approving, rejecting, and adjusting windows.
- Has a local Reset Demo control.

  - `pages/admin/equipment.html`

- Approval/rejection uses real API mutations.
- Settings use `/api/settings`.
- Dashboard uses `/api/dashboard`.
- Sidebar navigation is shared and normalized through `js/nav.js`.

### 14. Settings

Prototype:

- Stores settings locally.
- Supports loan duration and notification frequency.
- Does not persist settings to the server.

Git frontend:

- Reads from `/api/settings`.
- Updates through `/api/settings` with PATCH.
- Uses the backend’s supported fields:

  - `returnReminderHours`
  - `notifyStaff`
  - `notifyStudents`

### 15. Audit and outbox

Prototype:

- Displays local sample audit and outbox arrays.
- No persistence beyond localStorage.

Git backend:

- Creates audit records for workflow changes.
- Creates outbox events for operations such as request creation, approval, pickup, extension, and return.
- Exposes them through `/api/audit/...` and `/api/outbox`.
- The maintained frontend has a Frontend Health/admin surface documenting these integrations, while full notification delivery remains a backend expansion area.

- Prototype uses a single generated top navigation shell.
- Git frontend uses separate page headers and admin sidebars.
- Prototype uses sample icons and local visual placeholders.
- Git frontend uses backend-driven labels and real IDs.
- Prototype’s admin layout is a single console view.
- Git frontend separates admin functions into maintainable pages.
- Prototype’s cards and tables are directly generated by `pages.js`.
- Git frontend keeps markup in individual HTML files so existing functionality and debugging remain clearer.

Therefore, the following prototype features should not be copied directly into production without backend support:

- Mock student/admin role switching.
- Hardcoded availability.
- Local request approval.
- Local notifications.
- Fake equipment quantities.
- Fake audit/outbox data.
- Static booking IDs.
- Static pickup passes.
- Local-only reset behavior.

We need to update the design of the actual Media Lab Manager frontend to match the new Figma-designed frontend prototype, while preserving and correctly integrating the application's existing functionality and backend/database.

Work in the latest Git repository:
...\COMP350\Media Lab\Media-Lab_Manager

The repository contains the actual frontend and other project folders, including backend/server and database-related code. There is also a separate folder containing the new Figma-designed frontend prototype which is named 'Media Lab Prototype'. First, locate and inspect these folders rather than assuming their exact paths.
##1. Overall objective
The goal is to bring the new Figma design into the actual application without losing existing features or breaking the backend integration.

There are two important sources:

A. The separate Figma frontend prototype
- This is the visual/design reference.
- Its styling, layout, page structure, typography, colors, spacing, cards, navigation, buttons, forms, and overall aesthetic should guide the redesigned interface.
- It may contain temporary, hardcoded, or mock data and prototype-only behavior.
- It may include placeholder equipment, fixed cameras, sample users, or other sample content that does not match the real application's data model.
- Do not treat its hardcoded data or mock behavior as the authoritative application logic.

B. The latest Git repository
- This contains the actual application and its existing functionality.
- Its current frontend is the source of truth for existing user workflows, UI behavior, routes, and frontend interactions.
- Its backend, database, API adapter, and related server code are the source of truth for data structures, endpoint contracts, authentication, authorization, and persistence.
- Preserve and adapt these existing systems rather than replacing them with the prototype's mock implementation.

The final result should look like the Figma prototype, but behave like the real Media Lab Manager application.

##2. Inspect the project before changing anything
Before editing, inspect:
1. The actual frontend folder in the repository, especially its HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.
2. The separate Figma prototype folder and all of its relevant HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets.
3. The backend/server folder, including routes, middleware, authentication, and request/response formats.
4. The database schema, database commands, seed data, and any documentation that explains the data model.
5. The current API adapter and how each page calls the backend.
6. The current login/session handling and any protected-page behavior.
7. Any README or setup instructions relevant to running the app.

Compare the prototype with the actual frontend and produce a short plan before making changes. Identify:
- Which pages and visual components need to be redesigned.
- Which existing frontend features and workflows each page currently supports.
- Which prototype features are only visual or mock implementations.
- Which existing API endpoints and database fields each workflow depends on.
- Any differences or conflicts between the prototype and actual application.

Do not make assumptions about the backend or database. Inspect the actual code and use its real endpoint names, data fields, status values, and validation requirements.

##3. Scope and file organization

Make the design and integration changes in the actual frontend folder in the Git repository.

Keep the existing multi-page structure:
- Multiple HTML files are allowed and should remain separate where that is how the actual application is organized.
- Keep CSS in separate stylesheet files.
- Keep JavaScript in separate files.
- Preserve the existing folder and file organization where practical.
- Reuse shared CSS for common design elements instead of duplicating styles across pages.

Do not convert the application into one giant HTML file.

Do not replace the actual frontend folder with the Figma prototype folder. The prototype is a reference to adapt from, not a replacement for the actual application.

Do not delete the separate Figma prototype. Keep it available for comparison and reference.

Do not modify backend or database files just to make the new design easier to implement. If a backend change appears necessary, explain why and identify the exact requirement before changing it. Prefer adapting the frontend to the existing backend contract.

Do not commit or push any changes. I will review the result and handle Git operations separately.

## 4. Design requirements: match the Figma prototype

Recreate the Figma design as closely as practical in the actual frontend.

Preserve the prototype's visual identity and design decisions, including:
- Page layout and hierarchy
- Navigation style and placement
- Header and sidebar treatment, if present
- Typography and text hierarchy
- Colors, backgrounds, borders, shadows, and corner radii
- Spacing, alignment, sizing, and responsive layout
- Buttons, links, form controls, cards, tables, status labels, and modal/dialog styles
- Icons and other visual assets
- Loading, empty, error, success, and disabled states where shown or needed

Use the Figma prototype's design as the reference for appearance, but use the actual application’s labels, data, and workflows.

Do not make an unrelated redesign or introduce a different visual style.

Where the prototype has a component or page that is not present in the actual app, determine whether it corresponds to an existing application feature before adding it. Do not invent new product functionality without a clear basis in the existing app or design.

If the Figma design is incomplete for a particular page or state, follow the established design language from the prototype and retain the existing page's behavior and content.

## 5. Preserve existing application functionality

The redesigned frontend must retain all functionality that currently exists in the actual frontend and is supported by the backend.

Inspect the actual code to identify all existing features, event handlers, form validations, API calls, state changes, and navigation paths. Do not rely only on this checklist.

At minimum, examine and preserve the relevant workflows for:

### User workflows
- Login and session handling
- User identity and account information
- Equipment catalog
- Equipment availability and status
- Search, filtering, sorting, and equipment details
- Booking/request creation
- Request submission validation and confirmation
- Viewing active bookings and request history
- Pickup passes and pickup workflow
- Return workflow and recording return condition
- Damage reporting
- Extension requests
- Notifications
- User navigation and sign-out

### Admin workflows
- Admin authentication and authorization
- Dashboard and statistics
- Equipment management
- Request review
- Approving and rejecting requests
- Cancellation, if supported
- Pickup and return administration, if supported
- Damage and extension review, if supported
- Audit history
- Outbox or other admin views, if supported by the current application

This list is a guide. The actual repository determines which of these workflows exist and what each one does.

Do not remove a working feature simply because the Figma prototype does not show it. Find a suitable place for it in the new design while keeping its behavior intact.

Do not add decorative controls that appear functional but do nothing. Every visible interactive element should either perform its intended action or be clearly presented as disabled/unavailable.

## 6. Adapt the prototype's mock data to the real application

item.stdout:
## Media Lab Equipment Lending Software By Arja S, Joyal Liju Jacob, Murali Krishnan, Upasana Rai.
For COMP350: Software Design Practical 2026 ## Local application The only HTTP backend is `MLM.integration/server/server.py`. It serves the maintained frontend from `Media Lab Front` and uses the SQLite database in `MLM.Database/media-lab.sqlite`. ```powershell python MLM.integration/server/server.py ``` Login uses a Krea email and four-digit PIN. The PIN is persisted as an scrypt hash and sessions are persisted in SQLite. The browser receives only an HttpOnly session cookie; no bearer token is stored in browser storage. New accounts always start as students; staff roles must be assigned directly in the database by an administrator. For local HTTP development, run with `COOKIE_SECURE=false`. Production must run behind HTTPS with `COOKIE_SECURE=true` (the default). Google authentication is not implemented.

## Design changes

Implemented the Figma admin-settings design from node `2:1400` in the real frontend:

- Reworked the admin Settings page into the Figma-style layout:
  - Figma-inspired top navigation
  - 260px sidebar
  - Settings cards
  - Lending Policy, Notifications, and General Settings sections
  - Teal color system, cards, borders, spacing, toggles, and responsive behavior
- Updated admin navigation labels and active-state handling.
- Kept the existing multi-page frontend structure under `pages/`, `css/`, and `js/`.
- Preserved `/pages/...` routes because the backend/session logic depends on them.

## Functionality preserved

- Admin authorization remains enforced through `data-require-role="admin"`.
- Existing settings loading and saving still use the real API.
- Supported settings remain functional:
  - Standard loan duration
  - Return reminder frequency
  - Staff notifications
  - Student notifications
- Unsupported controls are visibly disabled instead of pretending to save data.

## Backend and database integration

No backend or database files were changed.

The Settings page continues using:

- `GET /api/settings`
- `PATCH /api/settings`

Static prototype values were removed. Server-managed values display as “Managed by server policy” unless returned by the backend.

## Authentication and security

- Existing session handling remains unchanged.
- Admin-only access is preserved.
- No prototype authentication bypass or mock login was copied.
- CSRF/API behavior remains handled by the existing API adapter.

## Files changed

- `Media Lab Front/pages/admin/settings.html`
- `Media Lab Front/css/admin.css`
- `Media Lab Front/js/settings.js`
- `Media Lab Front/js/nav.js`

No backend or database files were modified.

## Testing

Passed:

- JavaScript syntax checks for all frontend JS files
- `git diff --check`

Not run:

- Browser visual testing
- Live backend integration testing, because Python/backend execution was unavailable in this environment

## How to run

From the repository root:

```powershell
python MLM.integration/server/server.py
```

For local HTTP development:

```powershell
$env:COOKIE_SECURE="false"
python MLM.integration/server/server.py
```

Then open the local URL printed by the server.

## Remaining work

The provided Figma URL points specifically to the admin Settings screen. The implementation above applies that design to the corresponding real page. Other pages can be migrated using the same design system while preserving their existing API workflows.

The prototype structure is not impossible to use in the Git repository, but it is mainly designed as a visual demo rather than a production frontend.

The prototype has:

```text
assets/
css/styles.css
js/app.js
js/pages.js
admin.html
admin-settings.html
bookings.html
catalog.html
...
```

The Git repository separates functionality into page-specific HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files because it is connected to the real backend, database, authentication, and API contracts.

### Main limitations of transferring the prototype structure directly

#### 1. Prototype state is stored locally

The prototype uses mock data and browser storage such as `localStorage`.

For example, equipment, users, bookings, notifications, and requests are seeded in JavaScript. This means:

- Data is not loaded from the database.
- Multiple users do not see consistent data.
- Refreshing or clearing storage can reset the application.
- Changes are not authoritative.
- Admin actions do not truly affect backend records.

The Git repository must instead call real endpoints such as:

```text
/api/equipment
/api/requests
/api/settings
/api/requests/{id}/approve
/api/requests/{id}/return
```

Replacing the real API with the prototype’s local state would break the application.

#### 2. Authentication would become unsafe

The prototype has a local/demo login mode and can switch between student and admin views.

That is useful for demonstrating the UI, but it cannot replace the repository’s authentication flow.

The real application needs to preserve:

- Server-side sessions
- HttpOnly cookies
- Role checks
- Admin authorization
- Session expiry
- Login redirects
- CSRF protection

If the prototype’s `app.js` authentication behavior were copied directly, users could potentially access admin screens without backend authorization.

#### 3. `pages.js` is tightly coupled to prototype markup

The prototype dynamically builds most of the interface using JavaScript templates.

This creates problems when adapting it to the real application:

- DOM elements are generated only when `pages.js` runs.
- Event handlers depend on prototype-specific IDs and classes.
- Page navigation assumes prototype filenames and paths.
- Backend-driven content requires additional loading, error, and empty states.
- One change to a shared template can affect every page.

The Git repository currently has page-specific scripts such as:

```text
catalog.js
bookings.js
history.js
notifications.js
return.js
admin.js
settings.js
```

That makes it easier to connect each screen to the correct backend workflow.

#### 4. One global stylesheet creates side effects

The prototype uses one large `styles.css`.

That is convenient for a visual prototype, but in the real application:

- Admin styles can accidentally affect student pages.
- Form changes can affect tables and cards elsewhere.
- Responsive rules become harder to isolate.
- Debugging becomes more difficult.
- Page-specific states require increasingly complex selectors.

A shared design system is still useful, but the Git repository benefits from:

```text
global.css
catalog.css
bookings.css
history.css
admin.css
...
```

This allows common colors, typography, cards, and navigation to remain shared while keeping page-specific behavior isolated.

#### 5. Prototype data fields do not always match the database

The prototype contains fields such as:

```text
category
brand
quantity
availableUnits
image
```

The real database may expose a different structure. For example, the current equipment model is based on actual equipment records and statuses rather than the prototype’s richer mock object.

Directly copying prototype rendering could cause:

- Undefined fields
- Incorrect availability values
- Fake categories or quantities
- Wrong equipment IDs
- Invalid request payloads

The design can be copied, but the values must be mapped from the real API response.

#### 6. Prototype controls may look functional when they are not

Prototype buttons such as:

- Add to Booking
- Approve Request
- Extend
- View Pickup Pass
- Save Settings

may only update local state or display a mock result.

In the real application, each control must:

1. Validate input.
2. Call the correct endpoint.
3. Handle success and failure.
4. Refresh or update the UI from the server response.
5. Respect authorization and business rules.

This is one of the biggest reasons not to replace the real page scripts with `pages.js`.

#### 7. Error, loading, and empty states are incomplete

The prototype is usually populated with sample data, so it does not demonstrate:

- Empty equipment lists
- Failed API requests
- Expired sessions
- Unauthorized admin actions
- Backend validation errors
- Loading indicators
- Partial data responses

The Git repository must support these states because they occur in real use.

#### 8. File paths and protected-page behavior differ

The prototype links directly between root-level pages:

```text
catalog.html
admin.html
history.html
```

The actual repository uses paths such as:

```text
pages/catalog.html
pages/admin/equipment.html
pages/admin/settings.html
```

The backend and session middleware know about these routes. Moving everything to root-level prototype paths could break:

- Login redirects
- Protected-page checks
- Admin role routing
- Relative asset paths
- API/session initialization

This is why the visual style can be transferred without necessarily copying the exact file locations.

#### 9. The prototype’s admin and user experiences are simplified

The prototype can switch between student and admin views using a UI toggle. The real application cannot safely rely on a visual toggle.

The actual role must come from the authenticated session and backend authorization. The interface can provide navigation between user and admin areas only when the current session has the required role.

#### 10. Large-scale maintenance becomes harder

A single `pages.js` file can work for a small prototype, but it becomes difficult to maintain as the application grows:

- User workflows and admin workflows become mixed.
- Backend-specific code accumulates in one file.
- Testing individual pages becomes harder.
- A change to one component can break unrelated screens.
- Merge conflicts become more likely when multiple developers work on different pages.

### Why the Git repository front page can look different

The prototype’s front page is a static visual design. The repository’s front page must also handle:

- Real login submission
- Session validation
- Server redirects
- Authentication errors
- Protected routes
- Real user identity
- Backend availability

Therefore, the repository may need different markup or scripts even when it uses the same visual language.

The correct approach is:

```text
Prototype:
visual reference and interaction concept

Git frontend:
same visual design
+ real API calls
+ real authentication
+ real validation
+ real backend states
```

### Recommended approach

Use a hybrid structure:

- Keep the Git repository’s separate page and API files.
- Reuse the prototype’s visual system:
  - Colors
  - Typography
  - Spacing
  - Cards
  - Buttons
  - Navigation
  - Status badges
  - Form styling
- Extract shared prototype styling into `global.css`.
- Keep page-specific styles in separate files.
- Adapt prototype components into real API-backed page scripts.
- Preserve the repository’s existing `/pages/...` routes and authentication flow.

This provides the prototype’s appearance without importing its mock data, local authentication, or fragile single-file behavior.

- Extend
- View Pickup Pass
- Save Settings

may only update local state or display a mock result.

In the real application, each control must:

1. Validate input.
2. Call the correct endpoint.
3. Handle success and failure.
4. Refresh or update the UI from the server response.
5. Respect authorization and business rules.

This is one of the biggest reasons not to replace the real page scripts with `pages.js`.

#### 7. Error, loading, and empty states are incomplete

The prototype is usually populated with sample data, so it does not demonstrate:

- Empty equipment lists
- Failed API requests
- Expired sessions
- Unauthorized admin actions
- Backend validation errors
- Loading indicators
- Partial data responses

The Git repository must support these states because they occur in real use.

#### 8. File paths and protected-page behavior differ

The prototype links directly between root-level pages:

```text
catalog.html
admin.html
history.html
```

The actual repository uses paths such as:

```text
pages/catalog.html
pages/admin/equipment.html
pages/admin/settings.html
```

The backend and session middleware know about these routes. Moving everything to root-level prototype paths could break:

- Login redirects
- Protected-page checks
- Admin role routing
- Relative asset paths
- API/session initialization

This is why the visual style can be transferred without necessarily copying the exact file locations.

#### 9. The prototype’s admin and user experiences are simplified

The prototype can switch between student and admin views using a UI toggle. The real application cannot safely rely on a visual toggle.

The actual role must come from the authenticated session and backend authorization. The interface can provide navigation between user and admin areas only when the current session has the required role.

#### 10. Large-scale maintenance becomes harder

A single `pages.js` file can work for a small prototype, but it becomes difficult to maintain as the application grows:

- User workflows and admin workflows become mixed.
- Backend-specific code accumulates in one file.
- Testing individual pages becomes harder.
- A change to one component can break unrelated screens.
- Merge conflicts become more likely when multiple developers work on different pages.

### Why the Git repository front page can look different

The prototype’s front page is a static visual design. The repository’s front page must also handle:

- Real login submission
- Session validation
- Server redirects
- Authentication errors
- Protected routes
- Real user identity
- Backend availability

Therefore, the repository may need different markup or scripts even when it uses the same visual language.

The correct approach is:

```text
Prototype:
visual reference and interaction concept

Git frontend:
same visual design
+ real API calls
+ real authentication
+ real validation
+ real backend states
```

### Recommended approach

Use a hybrid structure:

- Keep the Git repository’s separate page and API files.
- Reuse the prototype’s visual system:
  - Colors
  - Typography
  - Spacing
  - Cards
  - Buttons
  - Navigation
  - Status badges
  - Form styling
- Extract shared prototype styling into `global.css`.
- Keep page-specific styles in separate files.
- Adapt prototype components into real API-backed page scripts.
- Preserve the repository’s existing `/pages/...` routes and authentication flow.

This provides the prototype’s appearance without importing its mock data, local authentication, or fragile single-file behavior.

content.text:
Implemented the hybrid frontend structure in the Git repository.

Changes made:

- Reworked `global.css` using the prototype’s visual system:
  - Teal color palette
  - Inter/system typography
  - Prototype spacing and card styles
  - Rounded buttons and status badges
  - Navigation styling
  - Form controls
  - Tables, cards, notices, booking layouts, pass layouts, and responsive behavior
  - Prototype-style shadows and backgrounds
- Preserved the existing separate page-specific CSS files.
- Preserved the existing API adapter, page scripts, authentication, and `/pages/...` routes.
- Updated admin navigation to use the Figma/prototype labels:
  - Catalogue
  - Requests
  - Equipments
  - Report
  - Settings
- Added active navigation states for admin pages.
- Kept Settings connected to the real `/api/settings` endpoints.
- Disabled settings controls that are not currently supported by the backend instead of making them appear functional.
- Removed hardcoded operating policy values and replaced them with backend-managed status text unless the API provides those values.

Files changed:

item.stdout:
--- database README ---
# Media Lab database module

This folder contains the SQLite data layer used by the backend. The Python implementation is mlm_database_commands.py and uses Python's built-in sqlite3 library.

## Initialize example data

From the repository root:

    python MLM.Database/seed_test_equipment.py

The initializer creates the schema if necessary and adds a consistent example set without deleting existing data. Running it again is safe: users, listings, equipment units, and example requests are identified and not duplicated. It creates four login accounts, ten catalog listings, 24 individually tracked equipment units, and examples of a pending request, an active loan, and a damaged return.

Example PINs:

- Alex Morgan: 2468
- Priya Shah: 1357
- Maya Chen (staff): 8642
- Demo Administrator: 9999

Set MEDIA_LAB_DB to initialize a different SQLite file. The initializer is for local/testing databases, not production data.

## Listings versus equipment

The listings table is the frontend catalog. One row represents a type of item and includes its quantity, category, location, and description.

The equipment table remains the authoritative inventory. Each physical unit has its own asset code, optional serial number, status, pickup history, return record, and damage reports. Equipment units link to a listing through listing_id.

For example, the catalog has one E27 LED Lightbulb listing with quantity 5, while the database has five separate E27 bulb equipment rows. If one bulb is damaged, only that unit becomes damaged and the listing reports four available units.

Database.get_listings() returns catalog rows with total_quantity, available_quantity, checked_out_quantity, equipment_ids, and available_equipment_ids. Individual equipment remains available through the existing equipment methods for staff-level inventory operations.

## Python use

    from mlm_database_commands import Database

    database = Database()
    listings = database.get_listings({"status": "available"})
    database.close()

Main operations include:

- Users: add_user, update_user, ban_user, unban_user
- Listings: add_listing, get_listings
- Equipment: add_equipment, update_equipment, find, stats
- Requests: check_availability, create_request, approve_request, reject_request, cancel_request
- Lending: record_pickup, mark_no_show, record_return, record_damage
- Backend support: get_dashboard, get_audit_history, get_outbox, mark_events_published

Request data normally moves through pending, approved, pickup_pending, picked_up, and returned. Rejection or cancellation releases equipment. A damaged return marks only the affected equipment unit as damaged.

## Output format

The module returns Python data structures, not formatted text:

- One record: a dict with database column names.
- Collections: a list of record dictionaries.
- Request results: a request dictionary containing items and windows lists.
- get_listings: catalog dictionaries containing quantity and availability counts plus unit ID lists.
- get_dashboard: a dictionary with pendingRequests, windows, and equipment lists.
- get_outbox: event dictionaries containing event type, aggregate ID, payload, and publication timestamps.

Use json.dumps(result) when an API needs JSON output. Dates must be ISO-8601 strings, and IDs are integer database IDs.

Call close() during process shutdown. Do not commit node_modules, SQLite database files, or generated logs. The original JavaScript command file remains available for compatibility.

/* Same-origin adapter for the single Python backend. Authentication is
   cookie-only: the session value never enters localStorage or sessionStorage. */
(function () {
  const base = (window.MLM_API_BASE || '/api').replace(/\/$/, '');
  let userCache = null;
  try { userCache = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem('mlmUser') || 'null'); } catch {}
  function redirectToLogin() {
    if (!/\/index\.html$|\/$/.test(location.pathname)) location.replace('/');
  }
  async function call(path, options = {}) {
    const method = String(options.method || 'GET').toUpperCase();
    const headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(options.headers || {}) };
    if (['POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'].includes(method)) headers['X-MLM-CSRF'] = '1';
    const response = await fetch(base + path, { credentials: 'include', ...options, method, headers,
      body: options.body && typeof options.body !== 'string' ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : options.body });
    const data = await response.json().catch(() => null);
    if (response.status === 401) {
      userCache = null;
      try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {}
      redirectToLogin();
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(data?.error || data?.message || `Request failed (${response.status})`);
    return data;
  }
  const json = (method, path, body) => call(path, { method, body });
  window.mlmApi = {
    base,
    login: body => json('POST', '/auth/login', { email: body.email, pin: body.pin }).then(data => {
      userCache = data.user || null;
      try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {}
      return data;
    }),
    logout: () => json('POST', '/auth/logout').finally(() => { userCache = null; try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {} }),
    me: () => call('/auth/me').then(data => { userCache = data.user || null; try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {} return data; }),
    currentUser: () => userCache,
    createUser: body => json('POST', '/users', body),

    createRequest: body => json('POST', '/requests', body),

    approveRequest: (id, _actorId, notes) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/approve`, { notes }),

--- database README ---
# Media Lab database module

This folder contains the SQLite data layer used by the backend. The Python implementation is mlm_database_commands.py and uses Python's built-in sqlite3 library.

## Initialize example data

From the repository root:

    python MLM.Database/seed_test_equipment.py

The initializer creates the schema if necessary and adds a consistent example set without deleting existing data. Running it again is safe: users, listings, equipment units, and example requests are identified and not duplicated. It creates four login accounts, ten catalog listings, 24 individually tracked equipment units, and examples of a pending request, an active loan, and a damaged return.

Example PINs:

- Alex Morgan: 2468
- Priya Shah: 1357
- Maya Chen (staff): 8642
- Demo Administrator: 9999

Set MEDIA_LAB_DB to initialize a different SQLite file. The initializer is for local/testing databases, not production data.

## Listings versus equipment

The listings table is the frontend catalog. One row represents a type of item and includes its quantity, category, location, and description.

The equipment table remains the authoritative inventory. Each physical unit has its own asset code, optional serial number, status, pickup history, return record, and damage reports. Equipment units link to a listing through listing_id.

For example, the catalog has one E27 LED Lightbulb listing with quantity 5, while the database has five separate E27 bulb equipment rows. If one bulb is damaged, only that unit becomes damaged and the listing reports four available units.

Database.get_listings() returns catalog rows with total_quantity, available_quantity, checked_out_quantity, equipment_ids, and available_equipment_ids. Individual equipment remains available through the existing equipment methods for staff-level inventory operations.

## Python use

    from mlm_database_commands import Database

    database = Database()
    listings = database.get_listings({"status": "available"})
    database.close()

Main operations include:

- Users: add_user, update_user, ban_user, unban_user
- Listings: add_listing, get_listings
- Equipment: add_equipment, update_equipment, find, stats
- Requests: check_availability, create_request, approve_request, reject_request, cancel_request
- Lending: record_pickup, mark_no_show, record_return, record_damage
- Backend support: get_dashboard, get_audit_history, get_outbox, mark_events_published

Request data normally moves through pending, approved, pickup_pending, picked_up, and returned. Rejection or cancellation releases equipment. A damaged return marks only the affected equipment unit as damaged.

## Output format

The module returns Python data structures, not formatted text:

- One record: a dict with database column names.
- Collections: a list of record dictionaries.
- Request results: a request dictionary containing items and windows lists.
- get_listings: catalog dictionaries containing quantity and availability counts plus unit ID lists.
- get_dashboard: a dictionary with pendingRequests, windows, and equipment lists.
- get_outbox: event dictionaries containing event type, aggregate ID, payload, and publication timestamps.

Use json.dumps(result) when an API needs JSON output. Dates must be ISO-8601 strings, and IDs are integer database IDs.

Call close() during process shutdown. Do not commit node_modules, SQLite database files, or generated logs. The original JavaScript command file remains available for compatibility.

/* Same-origin adapter for the single Python backend. Authentication is
   cookie-only: the session value never enters localStorage or sessionStorage. */
(function () {
  const base = (window.MLM_API_BASE || '/api').replace(/\/$/, '');
  let userCache = null;
  try { userCache = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem('mlmUser') || 'null'); } catch {}
  function redirectToLogin() {
    if (!/\/index\.html$|\/$/.test(location.pathname)) location.replace('/');
  }
  async function call(path, options = {}) {
    const method = String(options.method || 'GET').toUpperCase();
    const headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(options.headers || {}) };
    if (['POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'].includes(method)) headers['X-MLM-CSRF'] = '1';
    const response = await fetch(base + path, { credentials: 'include', ...options, method, headers,
      body: options.body && typeof options.body !== 'string' ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : options.body });
    const data = await response.json().catch(() => null);
    if (response.status === 401) {
      userCache = null;
      try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {}
      redirectToLogin();
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(data?.error || data?.message || `Request failed (${response.status})`);
    return data;
  }
  const json = (method, path, body) => call(path, { method, body });
  window.mlmApi = {
    base,
    login: body => json('POST', '/auth/login', { email: body.email, pin: body.pin }).then(data => {
      userCache = data.user || null;
      try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {}
      return data;
    }),
    logout: () => json('POST', '/auth/logout').finally(() => { userCache = null; try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {} }),
    me: () => call('/auth/me').then(data => { userCache = data.user || null; try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {} return data; }),
    currentUser: () => userCache,
    createUser: body => json('POST', '/users', body),
    users: () => call('/users'),
    equipment: (filters = {}) => call('/equipment?' + new URLSearchParams(filters)),
    addEquipment: body => json('POST', '/equipment', body),
    updateEquipment: (id, body) => call(`/equipment/${id}`, { method: 'PATCH', body }),
    stats: () => call('/equipment/stats'),
    createRequest: body => json('POST', '/requests', body),
    requests: (query = '') => call('/requests' + query),
    approveRequest: (id, _actorId, notes) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/approve`, { notes }),
    rejectRequest: (id, _actorId, reason) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/reject`, { reason }),
    cancelRequest: (id, _actorId) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/cancel`, {}),
    scheduleWindow: body => json('POST', `/requests/${body.requestId}/windows`, body),
    pickup: (id, body) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/pickup`, body),
    return: (id, body) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/return`, body),
    damage: body => json('POST', `/request-items/${body.requestItemId}/damage`, body),
    extension: body => json('POST', `/requests/${body.requestId}/extensions`, body),
    dashboard: () => call('/dashboard'),
    audit: (type, id) => call(`/audit/${encodeURIComponent(type)}/${id}`),
    outbox: () => call('/outbox'),
    settings: () => call('/settings'),
    updateSettings: body => call('/settings', { method: 'PATCH', body })
  };
  window.mlmUiError = message => { const toast = document.querySelector('#toast'); if (toast) { toast.textContent = message; toast.classList.add('show'); setTimeout(() => toast.classList.remove('show'), 3500); } else console.error(message); };
  window.mlmSessionReady = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (window.mlmSession) return resolve();
    const script = document.createElement('script');
    script.src = new URL('session.js', document.currentScript?.src || location.href).href;
    script.onload = resolve;
    script.onerror = reject;
    document.head.appendChild(script);
  });
})();

--- database README ---
# Media Lab database module

This folder contains the SQLite data layer used by the backend. The Python implementation is mlm_database_commands.py and uses Python's built-in sqlite3 library.

## Initialize example data

From the repository root:

    python MLM.Database/seed_test_equipment.py

The initializer creates the schema if necessary and adds a consistent example set without deleting existing data. Running it again is safe: users, listings, equipment units, and example requests are identified and not duplicated. It creates four login accounts, ten catalog listings, 24 individually tracked equipment units, and examples of a pending request, an active loan, and a damaged return.

Example PINs:

- Alex Morgan: 2468
- Priya Shah: 1357
- Maya Chen (staff): 8642
- Demo Administrator: 9999

Set MEDIA_LAB_DB to initialize a different SQLite file. The initializer is for local/testing databases, not production data.

## Listings versus equipment

The listings table is the frontend catalog. One row represents a type of item and includes its quantity, category, location, and description.

The equipment table remains the authoritative inventory. Each physical unit has its own asset code, optional serial number, status, pickup history, return record, and damage reports. Equipment units link to a listing through listing_id.

For example, the catalog has one E27 LED Lightbulb listing with quantity 5, while the database has five separate E27 bulb equipment rows. If one bulb is damaged, only that unit becomes damaged and the listing reports four available units.

Database.get_listings() returns catalog rows with total_quantity, available_quantity, checked_out_quantity, equipment_ids, and available_equipment_ids. Individual equipment remains available through the existing equipment methods for staff-level inventory operations.

## Python use

    from mlm_database_commands import Database

    database = Database()
    listings = database.get_listings({"status": "available"})
    database.close()

Main operations include:

- Users: add_user, update_user, ban_user, unban_user
- Listings: add_listing, get_listings
- Equipment: add_equipment, update_equipment, find, stats
- Requests: check_availability, create_request, approve_request, reject_request, cancel_request
- Lending: record_pickup, mark_no_show, record_return, record_damage
- Backend support: get_dashboard, get_audit_history, get_outbox, mark_events_published

Request data normally moves through pending, approved, pickup_pending, picked_up, and returned. Rejection or cancellation releases equipment. A damaged return marks only the affected equipment unit as damaged.

## Output format

The module returns Python data structures, not formatted text:

- One record: a dict with database column names.
- Collections: a list of record dictionaries.
- Request results: a request dictionary containing items and windows lists.
- get_listings: catalog dictionaries containing quantity and availability counts plus unit ID lists.
- get_dashboard: a dictionary with pendingRequests, windows, and equipment lists.
- get_outbox: event dictionaries containing event type, aggregate ID, payload, and publication timestamps.

Use json.dumps(result) when an API needs JSON output. Dates must be ISO-8601 strings, and IDs are integer database IDs.

Call close() during process shutdown. Do not commit node_modules, SQLite database files, or generated logs. The original JavaScript command file remains available for compatibility.

--- database README ---
# Media Lab database module

This folder contains the SQLite data layer used by the backend. The Python implementation is mlm_database_commands.py and uses Python's built-in sqlite3 library.

## Initialize example data

From the repository root:

    python MLM.Database/seed_test_equipment.py

The initializer creates the schema if necessary and adds a consistent example set without deleting existing data. Running it again is safe: users, listings, equipment units, and example requests are identified and not duplicated. It creates four login accounts, ten catalog listings, 24 individually tracked equipment units, and examples of a pending request, an active loan, and a damaged return.

Example PINs:

- Alex Morgan: 2468
- Priya Shah: 1357
- Maya Chen (staff): 8642
- Demo Administrator: 9999

Set MEDIA_LAB_DB to initialize a different SQLite file. The initializer is for local/testing databases, not production data.

## Listings versus equipment

The listings table is the frontend catalog. One row represents a type of item and includes its quantity, category, location, and description.

The equipment table remains the authoritative inventory. Each physical unit has its own asset code, optional serial number, status, pickup history, return record, and damage reports. Equipment units link to a listing through listing_id.

For example, the catalog has one E27 LED Lightbulb listing with quantity 5, while the database has five separate E27 bulb equipment rows. If one bulb is damaged, only that unit becomes damaged and the listing reports four available units.

Database.get_listings() returns catalog rows with total_quantity, available_quantity, checked_out_quantity, equipment_ids, and available_equipment_ids. Individual equipment remains available through the existing equipment methods for staff-level inventory operations.

## Python use

    from mlm_database_commands import Database

    database = Database()
    listings = database.get_listings({"status": "available"})
    database.close()

Main operations include:

- Users: add_user, update_user, ban_user, unban_user
- Listings: add_listing, get_listings
- Equipment: add_equipment, update_equipment, find, stats
- Requests: check_availability, create_request, approve_request, reject_request, cancel_request
- Lending: record_pickup, mark_no_show, record_return, record_damage
- Backend support: get_dashboard, get_audit_history, get_outbox, mark_events_published

Request data normally moves through pending, approved, pickup_pending, picked_up, and returned. Rejection or cancellation releases equipment. A damaged return marks only the affected equipment unit as damaged.

## Output format

The module returns Python data structures, not formatted text:

- One record: a dict with database column names.
- Collections: a list of record dictionaries.
- Request results: a request dictionary containing items and windows lists.
- get_listings: catalog dictionaries containing quantity and availability counts plus unit ID lists.
- get_dashboard: a dictionary with pendingRequests, windows, and equipment lists.
- get_outbox: event dictionaries containing event type, aggregate ID, payload, and publication timestamps.

Use json.dumps(result) when an API needs JSON output. Dates must be ISO-8601 strings, and IDs are integer database IDs.

Call close() during process shutdown. Do not commit node_modules, SQLite database files, or generated logs. The original JavaScript command file remains available for compatibility.

/* Same-origin adapter for the single Python backend. Authentication is
   cookie-only: the session value never enters localStorage or sessionStorage. */
(function () {
  const base = (window.MLM_API_BASE || '/api').replace(/\/$/, '');
  let userCache = null;
  try { userCache = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem('mlmUser') || 'null'); } catch {}
  function redirectToLogin() {
    if (!/\/index\.html$|\/$/.test(location.pathname)) location.replace('/');
  }
  async function call(path, options = {}) {
    const method = String(options.method || 'GET').toUpperCase();
    const headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(options.headers || {}) };
    if (['POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'].includes(method)) headers['X-MLM-CSRF'] = '1';
    const response = await fetch(base + path, { credentials: 'include', ...options, method, headers,
      body: options.body && typeof options.body !== 'string' ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : options.body });
    const data = await response.json().catch(() => null);
    if (response.status === 401) {
      userCache = null;
      try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {}
      redirectToLogin();
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(data?.error || data?.message || `Request failed (${response.status})`);
    return data;
  }
  const json = (method, path, body) => call(path, { method, body });
  window.mlmApi = {
    base,
    login: body => json('POST', '/auth/login', { email: body.email, pin: body.pin }).then(data => {
      userCache = data.user || null;
      try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {}
      return data;
    }),
    logout: () => json('POST', '/auth/logout').finally(() => { userCache = null; try { sessionStorage.removeItem('mlmUser'); } catch {} }),
    me: () => call('/auth/me').then(data => { userCache = data.user || null; try { sessionStorage.setItem('mlmUser', JSON.stringify(userCache)); } catch {} return data; }),
    currentUser: () => userCache,
    createUser: body => json('POST', '/users', body),
    users: () => call('/users'),
    equipment: (filters = {}) => call('/equipment?' + new URLSearchParams(filters)),
    addEquipment: body => json('POST', '/equipment', body),
    updateEquipment: (id, body) => call(`/equipment/${id}`, { method: 'PATCH', body }),
    stats: () => call('/equipment/stats'),
    createRequest: body => json('POST', '/requests', body),
    requests: (query = '') => call('/requests' + query),
    approveRequest: (id, _actorId, notes) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/approve`, { notes }),
    rejectRequest: (id, _actorId, reason) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/reject`, { reason }),
    cancelRequest: (id, _actorId) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/cancel`, {}),
    scheduleWindow: body => json('POST', `/requests/${body.requestId}/windows`, body),
    pickup: (id, body) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/pickup`, body),
    return: (id, body) => json('POST', `/requests/${id}/return`, body),
    damage: body => json('POST', `/request-items/${body.requestItemId}/damage`, body),
    extension: body => json('POST', `/requests/${body.requestId}/extensions`, body),
    dashboard: () => call('/dashboard'),
    audit: (type, id) => call(`/audit/${encodeURIComponent(type)}/${id}`),
    outbox: () => call('/outbox'),
    settings: () => call('/settings'),

+## Initialize example data
+
+From the repository root:
+
+    python MLM.Database/seed_test_equipment.py
+
+The initializer creates the schema if necessary and adds a consistent example set without deleting existing data. Running it again is safe: users, listings, equipment units, and example requests are identified and not duplicated. It creates four login accounts, ten catalog listings, 24 individually tracked equipment units, and examples of a pending request, an active loan, and a damaged return.

+Set MEDIA_LAB_DB to initialize a different SQLite file. The initializer is for local/testing databases, not production data.
+
+## Listings versus equipment
+
+The listings table is the frontend catalog. One row represents a type of item and includes its quantity, category, location, and description.
+
+The equipment table remains the authoritative inventory. Each physical unit has its own asset code, optional serial number, status, pickup history, return record, and damage reports. Equipment units link to a listing through listing_id.
+
+For example, the catalog has one E27 LED Lightbulb listing with quantity 5, while the database has five separate E27 bulb equipment rows. If one bulb is damaged, only that unit becomes damaged and the listing reports four available units.
+
+Database.get_listings() returns catalog rows with total_quantity, available_quantity, checked_out_quantity, equipment_ids, and available_equipment_ids. Individual equipment remains available through the existing equipment methods for staff-level inventory operations.

## Database/frontend comparison

The latest database commit introduced a new catalog model:

- `listings` represents catalog items.
- `equipment` represents individual physical units.
- Each equipment unit references a listing through `listing_id`.
- Listings include:
  - Name
  - Description
  - Category
  - Location
  - Quantity
  - Available quantity
  - Equipment IDs
  - Available equipment IDs

The database now distinguishes between a catalog item and its physical units. For example, one “E27 LED Lightbulb” listing can represent five individual equipment records.

However, the current backend server does not expose a `/api/listings` endpoint. It still exposes:

```text
GET /api/equipment
GET /api/equipment/stats
```

Therefore, the existing frontend was still receiving individual equipment records rather than catalog listings.

## Frontend adjustment made

The catalog frontend now groups equipment units into listing-style cards using:

```text
listing_id
```

If `listing_id` is unavailable, it falls back to the equipment name.

Each catalog card now displays:

```text
available units of total units available
```

For example:

```text
2 of 5 available
```

The cart still stores an actual available equipment ID, so booking requests remain compatible with the backend’s current request API.

The admin equipment page continues using individual equipment records because that page represents physical inventory management.

## Prototype SVG usage

The prototype assets were used in these locations:

| Asset | Prototype usage | Git frontend usage |
|---|---|---|

Media Lab Front/assets/line.svg

Media Lab Front/index.html

No database or backend files were modified.

- `git diff --check`

- Live backend test
- Browser visual testing
- Database seeding test

content.text:
## Changes made

### 1. Removed the Location column

The admin equipment table no longer displays the `Location` column.

However, `location` is connected to the backend/database:

- It exists in the `equipment` table.
- It is returned by `/api/equipment`.
- It is supported by the backend update method.
- It can still be edited through the equipment edit form.

Therefore, I removed it from the table for cleaner presentation but retained it in the edit form and backend data flow.

### 2. Implemented equipment editing

Previously, clicking Edit displayed a message because the frontend had no edit form, even though the backend already supported editing.

The existing API adapter already contains:

```javascript
updateEquipment(id, body)
```

which calls:

```text
PATCH /api/equipment/{id}
```

The edit button now opens a modal form containing:

- Equipment name
- Asset code
- Serial number
- Status
- Location
- Description

Saving the form:

1. Sends the update through the existing API adapter.
2. Uses the backend’s current update endpoint.
3. Updates the table using the returned equipment record.
4. Displays backend errors through the existing toast system.

No backend changes were needed.

### 3. Removed the redundant admin sidebar

The admin pages now use only the top navigation bar.

Removed visually and structurally:

- Left navigation sidebar
- Sidebar injection from `nav.js`
- Sidebar markup from the Requests and History pages

The top navigation still links to:

- Catalogue
- Requests
- Equipments
- Report
- Settings

Admin page authorization and routing remain unchanged.

### 4. Removed Frontend Health

The Frontend Health page was removed:

```text
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/frontend-health.html
Media Lab Front/js/frontend-health.js
```

It was originally added as a development diagnostic page to document frontend/backend wiring and known limitations. It did not provide live monitoring or backend health information, so it was not meaningful as a production admin feature.

All navigation references to it were removed.

### 5. Equipment return confirmation ideas

I did not implement this workflow, as requested.

The current backend return flow records a return directly through:

```text
POST /api/requests/{id}/return
```

That is not enough for a two-party confirmation workflow. A stronger design would be:

#### Student submission

The student submits:

- Claimed return date/time
- Equipment condition
- Damage description
- Damage photos
- Missing-item information

The request status becomes something like:

```text
return_submitted
```

The equipment should remain pending staff verification.

#### Media Lab verification

A staff member reviews:

- Actual physical return date/time
- Equipment condition
- Damage report accuracy
- Missing accessories
- Staff notes
- Verification photos, if needed

The staff member then chooses:

```text
verified_returned
verified_damaged
missing_items
disputed_return
```

#### Recommended backend additions

A future backend implementation could add:

- A `return_submissions` table
- `submitted_at`
- `verified_at`
- `verified_by`
- `actual_returned_at`
- `student_condition`
- `staff_condition`
- `staff_notes`
- `verification_status`
- Photo/file references

Possible endpoints:

```text
POST /api/requests/{id}/return-submission
GET /api/requests/{id}/return-submission
POST /api/requests/{id}/return-verification
```

The frontend could then provide:

- Student return submission form
- Admin pending-return review page
- Staff verification form
- Final status and notification after verification

This requires backend/database support and was intentionally not implemented.

## Files changed

```text
Media Lab Front/css/admin.css
Media Lab Front/js/admin.js
Media Lab Front/js/nav.js
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/equipment.html
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/history.html
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/requests.html
```

Removed:

```text
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/frontend-health.html
Media Lab Front/js/frontend-health.js
```

No backend or database files were changed.

## Validation

Passed:

- JavaScript syntax checks for all frontend JavaScript files
- `git diff --check`
- Confirmed no remaining Frontend Health references

Not run:

- Live backend/browser testing, because the backend was not started in this environment.

content.text:
Implemented the requested frontend/data-flow changes.

### Data and backend integration

Added two backend-supported frontend endpoints:

```text
GET /api/listings
GET /api/policy
```

`/api/listings` exposes database-backed catalog listings with:

- Total quantity
- Available quantity
- Checked-out quantity
- Category
- Location
- Equipment IDs

`/api/policy` exposes the configured standard loan duration to students without exposing admin-only settings.

The frontend API adapter now includes:

```javascript
mlmApi.listings()
mlmApi.policy()
```

No database schema changes were made.

### Equipment quantities

Student catalog quantities now come from `/api/listings`.

Admin equipment quantities now use the same database listing data, so both views display the same:

- Total quantity
- Available quantity
- Checked-out quantity

The admin page still uses individual equipment IDs for editing.

### Brand filters

Student and admin brand filters are now generated dynamically from backend-returned equipment/listing names.

There are no hardcoded Sony, Canon, Sigma, RØDE, or other brand filter options remaining in the catalog UI.

The database does not currently have a separate `brand` column. Brands are therefore derived from the database-provided listing/equipment names. A dedicated `brand` field would be needed if brand filtering must become fully authoritative.

### Extension requests

Added a functional extension request interface in the user booking history:

- Opens a proper extension dialog
- Shows booking and equipment details
- Allows selecting a new return date/time
- Requires a reason
- Submits through the existing extension endpoint
- Refreshes the booking history after submission

Admin requests now also display pending extension requests and provide:

- Approve extension
- Reject extension

These use the existing request-window API.

### Navigation and controls

Removed the catalog page’s redundant square notification and cart buttons.

For admins:

- The top navigation now labels the catalog link as `User View`.
- This makes it clear that it switches to the student-facing interface.
- Admin navigation remains available through the top bar.

Added a `Log out` button for authenticated users and admins. It calls the existing logout endpoint and redirects to the login page.

### Removed dashboard page

Removed:

```text
Media Lab Front/pages/admin/dashboard.html
Media Lab Front/js/admin-dashboard.js
```

All dashboard references were removed. The admin interface now starts from the equipment management page.

### Static information reduced

Removed static catalog brand lists and static notification counts.

Booking loan-duration text now comes from the backend policy endpoint.

Equipment/request quantities and request extension data are loaded from backend responses.

Some UI labels remain static because they describe actions or sections rather than application data.

### Files changed

Backend:

```text

```

Frontend:

Media Lab Front/js/admin.js

Media Lab Front/pages/admin/settings.html
Media Lab Front/pages/bookings.html

Media Lab Front/pages/notifications.html
```

Removed:

```text

Media Lab Front/js/admin-dashboard.js
```

Passed:

- JavaScript syntax checks for all frontend JavaScript files
- `git diff --check`
- Confirmed dashboard references were removed

Not run:

- Live Python backend test
- Browser workflow testing
- Database seeding test
